In 1876 the British planter Henry Wickham shipped about 70,000 seeds of the rubber tree, Hevea brasiliensis, from the Amazon near Santarém to London. Brazil then had a near monopoly on natural rubber, which bicycle tyres, and later car tyres, made ever more valuable.

The seeds went to Kew Gardens, where only a few thousand sprouted. Seedlings were sent on to Ceylon and Singapore, and from them grew the rubber plantations of British Malaya and the Dutch East Indies. Wickham told the story as a daring smuggle; whether any Brazilian law was broken is disputed, and Brazilians later called it biopiracy. He was knighted in 1920.

Trees planted in rows and tapped by migrant workers from southern India and China gave rubber far more cheaply than wild trees scattered through the forest. By about 1913 Asian plantations outproduced the Amazon, and the Amazon rubber boom collapsed. It is one of history's great plant transfers, like the silkworms smuggled to Byzantium.
